_meta.description: ALPR Abuse Library — curated index of news articles documenting ALPR misuse and civil liberties concerns

entries.title: Kechi police lieutenant arrested for using police technology to stalk wife
entries.description: Kechi Police Lieutenant Victor Heiar was arrested by the Wichita Police Department after it was discovered he utilized his position within the police department to unlawfully access WPD's Flock license plate reader technology to monitor where his estranged wife was located.

entries.title: Kansas police chief used Flock license plate cameras 164 times to track ex-girlfriend
entries.description: Sedgwick, Kansas police chief used Flock Safety license plate readers to track his ex-girlfriend and her new boyfriend's vehicles over 200 times and resigned after admitting to misusing the technology.

entries.title: City of Toledo reaches $35K settlement with man who said he was injured by police K-9 during traffic stop
entries.description: Flock camera misread a '7' on Brandon Upchurch's license plate as a '2,' generating a stolen vehicle alert. Officer Adrian Wilson initiated a felony stop, drew weapons, and released a police dog on Upchurch before confirming plate ownership. Upchurch was jailed and charged; charges were dropped in August 2024 and the city of Toledo settled for $35,000. The officer received only a verbal reprimand.

entries.title: After police used Flock cameras to accuse a Denver woman of theft, she had to prove her own innocence
entries.description: Columbine Valley Sgt. Jamie Milliman used Flock camera data to issue a summons to Denver financial advisor Chrisanna Elser for a package theft she did not commit. He refused to show her the alleged evidence and told her she had driven through town 20 times in the past month. Elser spent days compiling GPS records, dashcam footage, and tailor receipts to prove her innocence. Charges were voided more than two weeks later. Follow-up reporting revealed Milliman had previously been fired from a prior agency; his discipline in this case was limited to extra training.

entries.title: Sandy Springs police officer terminated after allegedly using city's Flock cameras for personal gain
entries.description: Reserve Sgt. Francis Esposito used his city Flock login to run license plates of multiple individuals and allegedly transferred the data to Signal 8, a private company he also worked for. A whistleblower former Signal 8 employee reported the data was used for beta testing and product validation. Esposito resigned during the investigation; Sandy Springs officially lists him as terminated and referred the case to the Georgia Peace Officer Standards and Training Council.

entries.title: ICE Can Reportedly Access Flock Surveillance Cameras — Now Americans Are Destroying Them
entries.description: With Flock's cameras feeding data to ICE, a grassroots revolt over who gets to watch whom is erupting on roadsides and in council chambers across the US. Covers camera destruction incidents in Oregon, Virginia, Illinois, and Connecticut, as well as cities that have terminated Flock contracts following community opposition.

entries.title: AI cameras are everywhere — and people are paying the price for their mistakes
entries.description: Business Insider reviewed police records, lawsuits, and local news coverage across more than a dozen cases nationally, finding that Flock ALPR misreads have resulted in people being stopped at gunpoint, sent to jail, and mauled by police dogs. Includes the Brandon Upchurch (Toledo) and Herron family (Morristown, TN) cases. Flock's stated accuracy is contested; IPVM independently found roughly 1-in-10 state misidentification rates in 2021 testing, after which Flock blocked further purchases for testing.

entries.title: License Plate Readers Lead to Wrongful Stops Across the Country
entries.description: Police held a Black family at gunpoint including children after an ALPR misread flagged their minivan as a stolen motorcycle. Officers forced them onto hot pavement before realizing the error. Body cam footage released publicly. The city settled for $1.9 million.

entries.title: ALPR Cameras in South Carolina: Flock Safety License Plate Readers
entries.description: Comprehensive investigative piece covering multiple South Carolina ALPR abuses: two sisters drawn on at gunpoint after a Flock camera wrongly flagged their rental car as stolen (lawsuit filed); 200+ Flock cameras installed on SC roads without SCDOT permits; a SLED officer who searched his own plate and altered the record to hide it; and the original Greenville Flock contract signed by Police Chief Kenneth Miller who was under an active SLED investigation and resigned weeks later using civil asset forfeiture funds to bypass council appropriations.

entries.title: Milwaukee Officer Charged in Flock Camera Misuse
entries.description: Milwaukee Officer Josue Ayala used Flock to query the license plate of someone he was dating 120+ times and a second plate belonging to that person's ex 55 times, entering only 'investigation' as justification. Ayala resigned as part of a negotiated plea agreement and was charged with a misdemeanor. The violations were discovered by one of the victims checking her plate on HaveIBeenFlocked.com, not through internal oversight. The same article covers Menasha Officer Cristian Morales, who used Flock while off-duty to track his ex-girlfriend, facing a felony misconduct charge.

entries.title: Georgia Police Chief Arrested for ALPR Stalking
entries.description: Police Chief Michael Steffman was arrested by the GBI on charges including stalking and violation of oath for using ALPR to stalk and harass multiple private citizens including searches of cameras in Capitola, California, thousands of miles from his jurisdiction. He resigned hours before his arrest, five days after being honored for 20 years of service.

entries.title: SC Lawmaker Wants Restrictions on Police Using Automatic License Plate Readers
entries.description: A domestic abuser falsely reported a partner as 'missing' to trigger ALPR alerts on their vehicle and use police infrastructure to track their whereabouts. Documented by SC Rep. Todd Rutherford as evidence supporting legislation to restrict ALPR use.

entries.title: Flock Gave Federal Immigration Agents Access to Tracking Data
entries.description: Flock gave U.S. Border Patrol an account to send data-sharing invitations to local police departments without notifying those agencies. 25 Colorado departments approved CBP access through batch approval without understanding what they were agreeing to. CBP gained access to 1,600+ plate readers across 22 states. CEO Garrett Langley denied any federal contracts on camera July 30, 2025, then admitted it August 19 after 9News forced the issue.

entries.title: Mountain View Police Turn Off License Plate Readers
entries.description: An audit revealed that Flock had enabled the nationwide search setting on Mountain View's system without the city's knowledge, exposing local data to hundreds of agencies including the ATF, Air Force, and GSA Inspector General none of whom had city authorization. The police chief immediately disabled cameras and the city terminated the contract.

entries.title: Illinois Audit Finds Flock in Violation of State Law
entries.agency: Flock Safety / Forest Park PD / Multiple IL agencies
entries.description: State audit found Flock gave CBP access to data from 12 local agencies in violation of Illinois state law, which bans sharing plate data with agencies investigating undocumented immigrants. Forest Park PD was separately sharing data with CBP through Motorola Solutions equipment. A suburban officer shared their Flock login with a DEA agent who conducted unauthorized searches. 47 agencies were removed from access to Illinois data following the audit.

entries.title: Leaving the Door Wide Open: Federal Access to Washington State ALPR Data
entries.description: UWCHR documented three modes of unauthorized federal access to WA ALPR data: 8 agencies explicitly authorized CBP sharing (front door), Border Patrol accessed data from 10+ agencies that never authorized sharing (back door), and local officers searched on behalf of federal agents using their own accounts (side door). Specific examples: Renton PD searched for Special Agent Michael R. Bonner (HSI); Richland PD searched 82 networks for HSI Investigation Intel; Auburn PD stated access occurred unknowingly to us.

entries.title: ICE Taps Into Nationwide AI-Enabled Camera Network
entries.description: Data obtained from Danville, IL police showed 4,000+ lookups nationally with search reasons citing immigration, ICE+ERO, or ICE WARRANT. Local officers searched on behalf of federal agents using their own accounts, providing ICE backdoor access to Flock's national network in circumvention of local sanctuary policies.

entries.title: Flock Safety Cameras Used for Federal Immigration Enforcement in Virginia
entries.description: VCIJ documented nearly 3,000 searches using terms ICE, ERO, immigration, and deportee on Virginia's Flock network over a 12-month period. In Bridgewater, VA (population ~6,000), just five cameras generated 6.9 million searches by outside agencies in 12 months, with 9 in 10 searches from out-of-state law enforcement.

entries.title: ATF Analyst Searched Richmond Flock Data Without Authorization
entries.description: An ATF analyst searched 49 plates through Richmond PD's Flock system without permission from the department, receiving 400 results over a quarter of which were related to an immigration case. The searches were conducted without Richmond PD's knowledge or authorization.

entries.title: Immigration Searches of Denver Flock Camera Data
entries.description: 1,400+ immigration-related searches of Denver's Flock data were conducted between June 2024 and April 2025. 80% of users accessing Denver's data were from outside DPD, including federal immigration agencies. This occurred despite Denver's sanctuary city status.

entries.title: ICE Taps Into School Security Cameras to Aid Trump's Immigration Crackdown
entries.description: Flock cameras installed in 100+ school systems for student safety were accessible to ICE through the same national network, allowing federal immigration enforcement agencies to query school camera data without the knowledge of school districts or parents.

entries.title: She Got an Abortion, So Texas Cops Used 83,000 Cameras to Track Her Down
entries.description: Johnson County deputies searched 83,345 cameras across 6,809 networks to track a woman who had a self-managed abortion, logging the search reason as had an abortion, search for female. The agency lied to access Massachusetts ALPR data, falsely claiming the vehicle was related to a stolen vehicle investigation. Flock initially defended the search as a legitimate missing-person case. Sheriff Adam King was subsequently indicted on unrelated felony charges.

entries.title: How Cops Are Using Flock Safety's ALPR Network to Surveil Protesters and Activists
entries.description: EFF analysis of 12 million searches logged by 3,900+ agencies between December 2024 and October 2025 found that 50+ federal, state, and local agencies ran hundreds of searches in connection with protest activity including the 50501 protests, Hands Off protests, and No Kings protests. In some cases, law enforcement specifically targeted known activist groups.

entries.title: EFF Investigations Expose Flock Safety Surveillance Abuses: 2025 Review
entries.description: EFF analysis found 80+ law enforcement agencies used racial slurs and ethnic stereotyping language targeting Romani people in Flock search reason fields. The year-end review also synthesizes EFF's 2025 investigations into immigration enforcement, protest tracking, and the Texas abortion case.

entries.title: Flock Safety Cameras Remained Active After Cities Asked Them Turned Off
entries.jurisdiction: Eugene, OR / Evanston, IL / Cambridge, MA
entries.description: Documents three cases of Flock cameras continuing to operate after shutdown orders: In Eugene, OR, at least one camera remained active weeks after officials ordered all 57 cameras off. In Evanston, IL, Flock reinstalled cameras without permission; the city sent a cease-and-desist. In Cambridge, MA, Flock installed 2 new cameras less than a month after the city council ordered 16 deactivated; Cambridge terminated the contract citing material breach of trust.

entries.title: Staunton to Cancel Flock Safety Camera Contract
entries.description: Flock CEO Garrett Langley sent an unsolicited email to all law enforcement clients characterizing community opposition as a coordinated attack. Staunton's 41-year police chief publicly rebuked Langley and the city terminated its Flock contract.

entries.title: Lawsuit Challenges San Jose's Warrantless ALPR Mass Surveillance
entries.description: SJPD logged 261,711 warrantless ALPR searches (~692/day) over a 12-month period. Including external agencies, total searches of San Jose's data reached 3,965,519. The city's cameras made 361 million plate scans in 2024; only 923,159 (0.2%) matched hot-list vehicles. EFF and ACLU-NC filed suit.

entries.title: Norfolk ALPR Mass Surveillance — IJ Case
entries.description: Lee Schmidt's car was logged 526 times in 3.5 months simply driving to work. Crystal Arrington's location was recorded 849 times. Neither was a suspect or under investigation. Norfolk police installed 172 cameras with the stated goal of making it difficult to drive anywhere of any distance without running into a camera somewhere. The Institute for Justice filed suit; a Virginia court later ruled ALPR surveillance does not require a warrant.

entries.title: California State Auditor Report on ALPR — LAPD
entries.description: State audit found LAPD had accumulated 320 million ALPR images. Only 400,000 generated an immediate match meaning 99.9% of stored images were of vehicles not on any hot list. LAPD retained all data for 5+ years and had no ALPR usage policy in place, despite state law requiring one since 2016.

entries.title: FBI Instructed Flock Users to Evade Audit Transparency
entries.description: A Houston HIDTA bulletin, forwarded by the FBI to its intelligence community, instructed Flock users to enter search reasons as vague as permissible, to exclude agencies that comply with public records laws from their data-sharing networks, and to limit searches to in-state to avoid jurisdictions that release audit logs.

entries.title: Flock Safety Strips Officer Names and Plates from Audit Logs
entries.description: After stalking officers were identified through audit log patterns, Flock unilaterally stripped officer names and license plates from the audit logs it provides to police agencies replacing unique identifiers with redacted and blocked VPN access to transparency portals. The company had previously described these logs as immutable and tamper-proof. A redaction error subsequently unmasked millions of surveillance targets.

entries.title: SC Sheriff Quoted Journalist $9,152 for Flock Audit Logs
entries.description: Richland County Sheriff's Department quoted a journalist $9,152 for two CSV files containing Flock audit logs the same files Florence County PD provided for free within one business day, and Bluffton PD mailed on a USB drive for $20. Documents the wide disparity in public records compliance across South Carolina agencies.

entries.title: Flock Denies Sharing Data with Private Investigators After Employee Comments
entries.description: A 9News investigation caught a Flock sales representative on a recorded Zoom call stating that Flock had previously been doing partnerships with private investigators or large investigative firms. Flock denied the claim after the recording was published, but the admission was on video.

entries.title: Flock Safety's Nova Platform: Dark Web Data Considered for Warrantless Tracking
entries.description: 404 Media reported Flock had been developing a platform called Nova to supplement ALPR data with information from data breaches and commercially available data to enable warrantless tracking of individuals. The EFF described it as a dystopian panopticon. After the reporting, Flock stated it had explored sourcing dark web/breach data but decided against it.

entries.title: Flock Rewrites Terms of Service to Claim Perpetual Data Rights
entries.description: Flock rewrote its Terms of Service twice in three months, making 147 documented changes. Key deletions: removed Flock does not own and shall not sell Customer Data; eliminated training data safeguards; added a perpetual data license; moved mandatory arbitration to Georgia; eliminated the gross negligence exception from liability caps; and restricted government termination rights.

entries.title: Researchers Claim Flock Cameras Are Easy to Hack — 51 Vulnerabilities Found
entries.description: Security researcher Jon Gaines demonstrated that anyone with physical access to a Flock camera can press a button sequence to create a Wi-Fi hotspot and gain root access to the device. Cameras run Android Things 8, discontinued by Google in 2021. 51 total security findings documented, 22 confirmed CVEs. Researcher Benn Jordan found Flock police login credentials for sale on dark web marketplaces. Flock does not require MFA for law enforcement accounts.

entries.title: Wyden and Krishnamoorthi Urge FTC to Investigate Flock Safety
entries.description: Senator Ron Wyden and Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi cited data from Hudson Rock showing at least 35 Flock customer law enforcement accounts had been stolen by hackers. Flock does not require MFA for police accounts. In at least one documented case, a DEA task force used a local detective's Flock credentials to conduct unauthorized searches.

entries.title: Sedona Council Terminates License Plate Reader Program
entries.description: Sedona's police department signed the Flock contract without notifying city council. Residents spotted cameras on social media. The mayor initially supported the cameras but reversed position after learning the scope of data sharing. Council voted unanimously to terminate the contract.

entries.title: Spartanburg Sheriff Chuck Wright Pleads Guilty to Federal Charges
entries.description: Sheriff Chuck Wright, who oversaw countywide Flock camera deployment, pled guilty to federal charges: conspiracy to commit theft from federal programs, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and obtaining controlled substances through fraud. He faces up to 30 years. Raises concerns about the integrity of ALPR oversight when the official responsible for the surveillance infrastructure is himself a criminal.

entries.title: Class Action Lawsuit Alleges Flock License Plate Readers Violate California Law
entries.description: Oakland law firm Gibbs Mura filed a class action lawsuit against Flock Safety in San Francisco Superior Court on February 26, 2026, alleging violations of California's ALPR Privacy Act. Out-of-state agencies searched SFPD's Flock database more than 1.6 million times in seven months. Oxnard PD suspended cameras after discovering a vendor-based issue had enabled nationwide access despite being set to California only. Ventura County found 364,000 unauthorized external searches. Plaintiffs seek $2,500+ per violation.

entries.title: Lenexa Police Investigated Op-Ed Writer Who Criticized ICE Response
entries.description: After Canyen Ashworth published a guest column criticizing Lenexa PD's failure to warn the community before an ICE raid, Police Chief Dawn Layman launched an investigation into him using the city's ALPR system to track his movements. Three weeks later, Layman issued a department-wide BOLO and internal directives telling officers to Make Your Own Case find any reason to stop him. No charges were filed. The ACLU of Kansas called it a wanton and disgraceful abuse of power. Chief Layman subsequently left for another department.

entries.title: What the Flock: Police Surveillance is Ripe for Abuse
entries.description: ACLU-WI analysis centered on Greenfield Police Chief Jay Johnson, facing felony misconduct charges for ordering installation of a department-owned surveillance camera outside his personal home during divorce proceedings after being explicitly told by the city attorney he could not. The piece also documents Wauwatosa PD conducting nearly 1,900 Flock ALPR searches in six months with the sole justification investigation, and synthesizes the broader pattern of ALPR domestic abuse.

entries.title: Border Patrol, DHS Accessed Woodburn Flock Camera Data, City Audit Shows
entries.agency: U.S. Border Patrol / DHS / Woodburn Police Department
entries.description: Despite earlier city assurances that Woodburn's Flock data was accessible only to Woodburn PD and Oregon law enforcement, a city audit confirmed DHS accessed Woodburn's camera data 175 times between March and May 2025, and Border Patrol conducted 209 searches between May and June 2025 all through a federal pilot program implemented by Flock without the city's knowledge. Cameras remain powered off with no reinstatement date.

entries.title: Dunwoody City Council faces public backlash over Flock camera data sharing practices
entries.description: Dunwoody City Council postponed a vote on renewing its $15,000 Flock contract after residents packed a meeting demanding accountability. Council Member Stacey Harris asked on record why 1,200 agencies can access Dunwoody's data and why SUNY is querying it. Flock's chief legal officer attended and promised contract revisions.

entries.title: Kansas Town Uses License Plate Readers to Go After Man Who Wrote Op-Ed
entries.description: ACLU Senior Policy Analyst Jay Stanley's analysis of the Lenexa/Ashworth case, adding significant detail: the police chief's Make Your Own Case directive instructing officers to manufacture a reason to stop Ashworth, First Amendment implications of selective enforcement, and the town's admission it had no formal poster policy. Frames the case as a textbook example of how mass surveillance infrastructure enables show me the man, I'll find you the crime policing.

entries.title: Joplin officer no longer employed after alleged misuse of license plate tracking system
entries.description: A Joplin officer was separated from the department after allegedly searching a single license plate approximately 395 times in violation of department policy. The abuse was discovered by a community member from Deflock Joplin reviewing publicly accessible Flock audit data not through internal oversight. The department referred potential criminal charges to the Missouri Highway Patrol and announced new monthly audit protocols.

entries.title: KBI: Ex-detective misused police resources to track spouse; child sex abuse material found
entries.description: Former Bonner Springs Detective Kyle Rector, 39, was arrested by the KBI after being suspected of using department resources on duty to monitor and stalk his spouse. During the investigation, child sexual abuse material was also discovered. Charges include five counts of sexual exploitation of a child under 14, five counts of breach of privacy, two counts of unlawful acts involving computers, one count of stalking, and five counts of official misconduct. Rector is held on $150,000 bond.

entries.title: Thornton Police Looking Into Complaint That Officer Ran Nearly 20,000 Flock Searches
entries.description: Community watchdog group Thornton For All filed an ethics complaint after discovering a single Flock account had conducted 19,194 searches between October 2023 and December 2025, with only 29 tied to case numbers (fewer than 1%). The account was identified through public audit data on HaveIBeenFlocked.com. Additional concerns centered on a potential conflict of interest: the officer's spouse serves as the department's public information officer. Thornton PD announced new weekly auditing protocols.

entries.title: ALPRs and Minneapolis' Growing Discriminatory Surveillance Dragnet
entries.description: Investigative report documenting MPD's deployment of 30 fixed Flock ALPR cameras across Minneapolis intersections, supplemented by approximately 70 additional privately-owned ALPRs at retail locations. In a two-month window (January-March 2026), these cameras logged data on more than 31 million vehicle passes. Of those, only 12,446 generated a hot-list match.

entries.title: Former Orange County Officer Pleaded Guilty to Using Police Database to Track Mistress, Harassing Her with Thousands of Texts and Phone Calls
entries.description: Former Costa Mesa officer Robert Jay Josett, 35, pleaded guilty on April 14, 2026 to unauthorized computer access, harassment by repeated contact, and contempt of court. Between June and December 2023, Josett used both CLETS and the department's Flock ALPR system to track his mistress and her partners. After being placed on leave in December 2023, he continued accessing the Flock system illegally. He was sentenced to three years of informal probation and a 52-week domestic violence program.

entries.publication: WHRO / Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism
entries.title: Virginia Police Search Vehicle Surveillance Data 24/7. 'Why?' Isn't Always Clear.
entries.description: VCIJ at WHRO analyzed 200,000 Flock search logs from nearly 150 Virginia law enforcement agencies covering July-October 2025. Despite Virginia's new ALPR law requiring specific stated purposes, officers routinely used abbreviations (CJ, inv, T) and single-word reasons. More than 1,800 searches used vague suspicious variants. Virginia agencies also continued sharing data with 800 out-of-state agencies in apparent violation of the new law.

entries.title: No Permit, No Problem: Riverside County's 500+ Unauthorized Surveillance Cameras
entries.agency: Riverside County Sheriff's Department / Flock Safety
entries.description: A CPRA records request revealed Riverside County issued three encroachment permits for 500+ Flock cameras all to the wrong permittee, improperly triggering a public-agency fee exemption that a private company should not have qualified for. The permits also lacked required traffic control plans. Between the first and second permits, cameras operated for over 13 months with no valid permit at all.

entries.title: RPD discloses sergeant violated Flock camera policy by sharing info with federal agent
entries.description: A Q1 2026 audit of RPD's Flock system revealed a sergeant shared ALPR data with an FBI special agent investigating a Washington, D.C. homicide in violation of department policy and Virginia state law, which generally prohibits sharing ALPR data with agencies conducting out-of-state investigations. Commonwealth's Attorney Colette McEachin declined to prosecute. The sergeant's Flock access was deactivated following an internal investigation. RPD announced quarterly public disclosure of future compliance findings.

entries.title: Not a one-off: More Coloradans stopped by police after data errors triggered Flock alerts
entries.jurisdiction: Boulder County, CO / Jefferson County, CO
entries.agency: Boulder County Sheriff's Office / Jefferson County Sheriff's Office / Aurora Police Department
entries.description: 9News follow-up documenting two additional victims of ALPR database errors beyond the earlier Dausman case. Sarah Judson, 76, was repeatedly flagged after Flock cameras matched her plate to a stolen vehicle report from Colorado Springs; a deputy later found her in a restaurant parking lot and told her two other officers were actively searching for her. Katie Rothman's plate had been entered into CCIC with a single-character typo by Aurora PD in 2023 and the error sat in the system for nearly two years. A Colorado bill to require warrants before querying historical ALPR data failed in the legislature the same week.

entries.title: Dayton suspends automated license plate readers after 'egregious' data sharing violations
entries.description: Dayton PD indefinitely suspended its Flock ALPR program after an internal review found a former Support Services Division commander had failed to implement required safeguards restricting external data access resulting in 7,100 immigration-related search requests from outside agencies in violation of city policy. City Manager Shelley Dickstein described the failures as egregious violations of policy. The violations were discovered in October 2025; all outside sharing was cut off by April 2026. The city will not proceed with a previously approved 27-camera expansion pending independent review.

entries.title: Former police officer who tracked estranged wife's car pleads guilty to stalking
entries.description: Former Frazer Township Officer Michael McSherry pleaded guilty to stalking and official oppression after using the department's license plate reader to track his estranged wife and her mother. His wife told the court McSherry tracked her over 250 times and had monitored the family for nearly a decade using GPS devices, nanny cams, and social media threats in addition to the ALPR system. McSherry was sentenced to 11.5 to 23 months in prison plus five years' probation, one of the earliest documented criminal convictions involving ALPR misuse for domestic stalking.

entries.title: Ex-RSO deputy who stalked former fiancee, harassed volunteer sentenced
entries.description: Former Riverside County Sheriff's Deputy Alexander Ravy Vanny, 35, was sentenced to six years in state prison after a December 2025 jury conviction on charges including stalking, unauthorized use of protected electronic data, illegal use of a tracking device, possession of child pornography, witness intimidation, and illicit eavesdropping. Vanny used the department's Flock ALPR system and physical GPS trackers to monitor his former fiancee after their split in summer 2024, forced her into his vehicle without consent, and continued offending while on bail. Prosecutors noted Vanny knowingly abused law enforcement access to facilitate the stalking.

entries.title: Affidavit: Deputy used SCSO database to track ex-wife's location without her knowledge
entries.description: Shelby County Sheriff's Deputy Thadius Gordon, 38, was relieved of duty with pay after his ex-wife reported he had used law enforcement ALPR databases to search her Tennessee license plate over 100 times approximately 20 times in a single four-day span without her knowledge. Gordon faces stalking and harassment charges. The SCSO Chief Deputy acknowledged the database could be misused and announced a review of policies and procedures.

entries.title: Former LMPD officer charged with official misconduct, stalking, harassment
entries.description: Former LMPD Officer Roberto Cedeno, 25, was indicted on nine charges including first-degree stalking, first-degree unlawful access to a computer, tampering with public records, and official misconduct, after LMPD's Public Integrity Unit found he had used the city's ALPR system and other law enforcement databases to track an ex-partner and her associates hundreds of times over two months. Cedeno resigned on April 8, 2025 before his termination was complete, then was separately arrested for violating a protective order while the investigation was still ongoing.

entries.title: Jerome County sheriff used Flock cameras to search for wife's vehicle, documents show
entries.description: Jerome County Sheriff George Oppedyk used Flock cameras to search for his wife's vehicle more than 700 times between July and September 2025, just months after the system went live, labeling the searches as test. A lieutenant detected the anomaly and notified the Idaho Attorney General's Office, which issued a subpoena and conducted a multi-month investigation. The AG found insufficient evidence to prove a crime, accepting Oppedyk's stated rationale of system reliability testing. Twin Falls Police briefly suspended Jerome County's cross-network access and required Oppedyk's removal from the system before restoring it. Oppedyk announced his retirement in March 2026, leaving office two years before the end of his four-year term.

entries.title: KCE Editor Files John Doe Petition Seeking Criminal Investigation Into Former Kenosha Deputy Over Alleged Database Misuse
entries.description: Former Kenosha County Sheriff's Deputy Frank McGrath resigned with severance pay after an internal investigation found he conducted approximately 16 Flock ALPR searches on a single day, all labeled Suspicious with no case number, and accessed the department's Polaris squad-vehicle GPS tracking system roughly 40 times while off-duty, apparently to track a coworker with whom he had a personal relationship. The sheriff's office never referred the matter to the DA, which told the Kenosha County Eye it had never been notified. The publication's editor filed a John Doe petition in Kenosha County Circuit Court seeking a judge to appoint a special prosecutor, citing a pattern of similar Wisconsin cases that had resulted in criminal charges elsewhere.

entries.title: Police officer allegedly used department database to stalk woman he met on TV set
entries.description: Monroe County Sheriff's Deputy Lamar Eliseo Roman, 28, was fired and arrested after using law enforcement databases including placing the woman's plate on a hotlist to track a complete stranger he had met as an extra on the Apple TV+ production Bad Monkey filming in the Florida Keys. Roman cat-called the woman on set, later messaged her on Instagram after she showed no interest, then used the department's ALPR system to create an alert that would notify him when her vehicle passed a camera, with the apparent goal of engineering a traffic stop. The Institute for Justice identified this as the most distinctive of 14 nationally documented officer ALPR stalking cases specifically because the target was a stranger, not a former intimate partner.

entries.title: Milwaukee police investigating second former officer for alleged misuse of license plate reader database
entries.description: Milwaukee police opened an investigation into a second former officer for alleged ALPR misuse, coming approximately three months after a different officer was fired for using the system to stalk an ex-partner. The back-to-back cases raise questions about internal oversight and access controls within the department.

entries.publication: State of Wisconsin v. Josue Ayala (Criminal Complaint)
entries.title: Criminal Complaint: State of Wisconsin v. Josue Ayala
entries.description: Primary source criminal complaint charging Milwaukee Officer Josue Ayala with attempted misconduct in public office for unauthorized ALPR queries on a victim's license plate. The complaint documents that the victim discovered she had been surveilled by checking her plate on haveibeenflocked.com, a notable instance of a civilian accountability tool directly surfacing law enforcement misuse of Flock data.

entries.title: Federal immigration agents accessed Syracuse drivers' data through secret Flock Safety deal
entries.description: A follow-up investigation by Central Current found that Syracuse PD had inadvertently enrolled in Flock Safety's nationwide data-sharing network, exposing driver location data to thousands of law enforcement agencies. A separate investigation revealed Flock's contract language allows the company to retain anonymized user data in perpetuity for its own commercial purposes, even if a municipality cancels its contract -- despite Flock's repeated public assurances that customers are the sole owners of their data.
entries.notes: Submitted by the reporter. Agency field corrected from 'Central Current' (publication) to 'Syracuse Police Department.' Description rewritten from submitter's raw text; inline URLs moved to additional_urls.

entries.title: License Plate Surveillance Logs Reveal Racist Policing Against Romani People
entries.agency: 80+ agencies, including Lake County SO (IL), Sacramento PD (CA), Palos Heights PD (IL), Irvine PD (CA), Fairfax County PD (VA), Grand Prairie PD (TX)
entries.description: EFF analysis of Flock Safety audit logs from more than 80 law enforcement agencies found officers conducted hundreds of ALPR searches using ethnic slurs and stereotypes targeting Romani people, often without specifying any crime. Search reasons included terms such as 'g*psy vehicle,' 'possible g*psy,' and 'g*psy ruse.' The Grand Prairie (TX) PD used Flock's Convoy feature -- which identifies vehicles traveling together -- to target a traveling Romani community as a group. Several agencies acknowledged the inappropriate language after EFF inquiry; Fairfax County PD defended the practice.
entries.notes: Submitted by Lucy Parsons Labs. Category corrected from 'racism' (not a schema category) to dragnet_surveillance + other. Jurisdiction broadened from 'Skokie' (not mentioned in article) to nationwide. Agency field expanded to reflect multi-agency scope. Description written by editor from source article.

entries.title: 2 Greer officers terminated for violating policy on Flock cameras, police say
entries.description: Greer Police officer Lynch was fired after using Flock cameras to search for a fellow officer he was romantically involved with, logging the searches under false pretenses such as 'welfare checks' and 'city planning.' A second officer, Echeverry, was also terminated for searching several citizens' plates and logging the reason as 'alcohol offenses' when that was not true.

entries.title: Georgia cops' alleged misuse of Flock license plate tracking data fuels privacy concerns
entries.jurisdiction: Greene County, Cherokee County, and Albany, GA
entries.description: At least ten Georgia police officers have been arrested and charged with misusing the Flock license plate reader database for personal reasons, spanning departments in Greene County, Cherokee County, and Albany. Flock's co-founder attributed the misuse to individual human conduct rather than the technology, while the ACLU of Georgia raised broader concerns about oversight and access controls.
entries.notes: Date published corrected from submitter's 2024-07-09 to 2026-07-09 (article is part of a July 2026 wave of Georgia coverage, confirmed via search). data_breach category dropped per editorial review; excerpt describes unauthorized use by authorized personnel, not a data exposure/leak.

entries.title: ICE accessed Capitola license plate data. Police say it was a mistake.
entries.description: Capitola police shared license plate reader data across state lines in a manner that unwittingly violated California state law restricting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. The department characterized the sharing as an unintentional error rather than a deliberate policy.

entries.title: Metro Atlanta deputies fired, arrested, accused of misusing license plate readers
entries.description: Three Cherokee County Sheriff's Office deputies were fired and arrested after an internal investigation found they had misused the Flock license plate reader database.

entries.title: Automotive journalist surrounded by police due to Flock camera confusion
entries.description: Automotive journalist Joel Feder and his wife were boxed in by four Plymouth, MN squad cars and detained after a Flock camera flagged their Range Rover press vehicle as stolen. The alert traced back to a data-entry error at a California agency that mis-keyed a lost manufacturer plate as stolen, causing multiple JLR press vehicles nationwide with similar plate patterns to be flagged.

entries.title: Sherwood stop sparked after Flock camera misread plate by one letter as stolen
entries.description: A Flock camera in Sherwood, AR flagged a vehicle as stolen after misreading its plate by a single character (APX 55X read as the stolen plate APX 55Y). Officers conducted a gunpoint stop in a Kohl's parking lot, detaining the driver and a passenger seated next to a one-month-old infant, before releasing them once the discrepancy was discovered.

entries.title: Sumter County suspends license plate reader program after detective accused of misuse
entries.description: Sumter County, FL Detective Brandy Almany was fired and criminally charged after an internal audit found she used the Flock ALPR system, along with the state driver database and a case-management system, to gather information on her husband's ex-wife, allegedly fabricating case numbers to disguise the searches as legitimate investigations. Sheriff Pat Breeden suspended the agency's entire Flock program pending a full audit.
